title: Sargable Predicates: Keep the Column Bare
description: Wrapping a column in a function makes a predicate non-sargable and forces a scan; keep the column bare so the index can seek. Why it matters: wrapping a column in a function is one of the most common, hardest-to-spot ways developers accidentally disable an index they assume is working.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
This lesson introduces one of the most important ideas in SQL performance: the difference between a filter the database *can* use an index for, and one it *can't* — even when the index exists. A filter that plays nice with indexes is called **sargable** (a weird-sounding word that just means "Search ARGument ABLE," i.e. usable as a search argument).

Why does this problem happen? An index is basically a sorted list of raw column values, like a sorted deck of cards. To use it, SQL Server needs to compare your filter directly against those raw values. The moment you do math or apply a function to the *column itself* before comparing it — like `Balance * 1.10 > 110000` — SQL Server can no longer just look up "110000" in the sorted list, because the index doesn't contain multiplied values, it contains the original ones.

Think of it like this: your index is a phone book sorted by name. If you ask "find everyone whose name, doubled, equals 'JohnJohn'," the sorted-by-name structure is useless — you'd have to check every entry and do the doubling yourself. That's exactly what happens here: because the math is on the column side, the database gives up on the index and reads every row instead. The fix is almost always to flip the math onto the constant instead, keeping the column bare so the index stays usable.

## Scenario
Finance wants accounts whose balance, after a 10% projected interest bump, would exceed 110,000: `WHERE Balance * 1.10 > 110000`. There's an index on `Balance`, but the 200k-row table is scanned every time even though only ~50 rows qualify.

## Why it's slow
Doing arithmetic on the **column** (`Balance * 1.10`) makes the predicate **non-sargable**. SQL Server would have to multiply every row before it could compare, so it can't use the `Balance` index to *seek* a range — it can only **scan** every row (an **Index Scan** of the whole Balance index).

## What to look for
- An **Index Scan** (reads all rows) instead of an **Index Seek**.
- Logical reads across the whole table for a query returning a handful of rows.

## The concept
Algebraically move the operation to the **constant** side so the column stays bare: `Balance * 1.10 > 110000` becomes `Balance > 100000` (divide both sides by 1.10). Now the index seeks straight to the ~50 qualifying rows. Rule of thumb: never wrap an indexed column in a function or arithmetic inside a `WHERE`/`JOIN` predicate.
hints: IX_Accounts_Balance exists but isn't used. What is being done to the Balance column?
Balance * 1.10 applies arithmetic to the column, making it non-sargable.
Rearrange so the column is bare: Balance * 1.10 > 110000 is the same as Balance > 100000.
